We need to propose a retrosynthesis route with 1 reaction for target SMILES: [CH2:1]=[C:2]([c:3]1[cH:4][cH:5][cH:6][cH:7][cH:8]1)[C@@H:9]1[CH2:10][CH2:11][CH2:12][C@@:13]1([OH:14])[C:15]([F:16])([F:17])[F:18]

Let's decode: It's a molecule with a styrene-like double bond attached to a cyclopentanol bearing CF3 group? Actually structure: CH2= C( aromatic phenyl ) attached to chiral carbon of cyclopentane bearing OH and CF3. So target is a product of carbonyl-ene reaction: forward reaction: carbonyl (ketone) + alkene -> allylic alcohol (hydroxyl) and new C-C bond, forming five-membered ring? Wait carbonyl-ene reaction between a carbonyl and an alkene within same molecule leads to intramolecular cyclization forming a five-membered ring and an alcohol. So retrosynthesis: break the C-O bond formed (the OH) and break the C-C bond formed (the new bond). The reverse step would be a carbonyl-ene reaction forward, so retrosynthetic step is to disconnect to a ketone and an alkene precursor.

Thus we need to propose a precursor that is a ketone with an alkene side chain that can undergo intramolecular carbonyl-ene to give the product.

Our target: a cyclopentanol fused to a side chain containing a phenyl-substituted alkene. The new bond formed is between the carbonyl carbon (of ketone) and the terminal carbon of the alkene? In carbonyl-ene, the alkene's allylic hydrogen transfers to carbonyl oxygen, forming OH, and the alkene carbon attaches to carbonyl carbon. So the product has a new C-C bond between the carbonyl carbon and the alkene carbon (the one bearing the allylic hydrogen). The OH ends up on the carbonyl oxygen (now alcohol). So the precursor would be a ketone with an alkene attached such that the carbonyl carbon is adjacent to the alkene? Let's think: In product, we have a cyclopentane ring with OH at carbon 13 (attached to carbon 13). The carbon bearing OH is also attached to CF3 and to carbon 9 (the chiral carbon attached to the alkene). The carbon 9 is attached to CH2= C(Ph) group. So the new bond formed is between carbon 13 (former carbonyl carbon) and carbon 9 (allylic carbon). The carbonyl oxygen becomes OH at carbon 13. The allylic hydrogen from carbon 10? Actually the allylic hydrogen is transferred from carbon 10 (CH2) to oxygen. In product, carbon 10 is part of the cyclopentane ring (CH2). So the precursor likely is a ketone at carbon 13 (C=O) attached to the cyclopentane, and an alkene side chain attached to carbon 9 (same as product). The carbonyl carbon is attached to carbon 9 via a single bond in product; in precursor, carbonyl carbon is double bonded to O, and attached to carbon 9? Wait carbonyl carbon is part of the cyclopentane ring? In product, carbon 13 is part of the ring, attached to carbon 12 and carbon 9 and OH and CF3. In precursor, carbon 13 would be carbonyl carbon (C=O) attached to carbon 12 and carbon 9 and CF3, but carbonyl carbon cannot be attached to carbon 9 and carbon 12 simultaneously because carbonyl carbon is sp2 with two substituents. In a cyclopentanone, carbonyl carbon is part of ring, attached to two ring carbons. Here we have a cyclopentanol with CF3 substituent; the carbon bearing CF3 is also carbonyl carbon in precursor. So precursor is a cyclopentanone with CF3 at carbonyl carbon? That seems unusual: a carbonyl carbon bearing CF3 (trifluoromethyl ketone). So precursor: CF3-CO- (attached to cyclopentane). The carbonyl carbon attached to carbon 12 and carbon 9 (makes a 5-membered ring). So the precursor is a 5-membered cyclic ketone (a cyclopentanone) with CF3 at carbonyl carbon (i.e., a trifluoromethyl ketone). The alkene side chain is attached to carbon 9 (which is adjacent to carbonyl carbon). The alkene is CH2=C(Ph)- (styrene). So the precursor SMILES: O=C(C(F)(F)F)C1CCCC1C=Cc1ccccc1? Wait need to place CF3 on carbonyl carbon: O=C(C(F)(F)F)C1CCCC1C=Cc1ccccc1? But carbonyl carbon attached to CF3 and to C1 (part of ring). The ring: C1CCCC1 attached to carbonyl carbon at position? Actually cyclopentanone: O=C1CCCC1. If we add CF3 to carbonyl carbon, we get O=C(C(F)(F)F)C1CCCC1. Then we need an alkene attached to the carbon adjacent to carbonyl carbon (the alpha carbon). In cyclopentanone, carbonyl carbon is part of ring; the adjacent carbon (alpha) is one of the ring carbons. In product, the alkene is attached to carbon 9 which is the carbon adjacent to carbonyl carbon (alpha). So we need a substituent on that alpha carbon: C=Cc1ccccc1 (styrene). So the precursor SMILES: O=C(C(F)(F)F)C1CCC(C=Cc2ccccc2)CC1? Let's construct: start with cyclopentanone: O=C1CCCC1. Add CF3 to carbonyl carbon: O=C(C(F)(F)F)C1CCCC1. Then add substituent at carbon 2 (alpha) which is the carbon after carbonyl in SMILES: maybe O=C(C(F)(F)F)C1CC(C=Cc2ccccc2)CC1. That yields a cyclopentanone with CF3 and styrene side chain. This seems plausible.

Now we need to find a template ID that matches carbonyl-ene reaction. Use search with functional_groups_broken: ["ketones","C-C double bonds"] and formed: ["aliphatic hydroxyls","five-membered rings"] maybe. Already attempted with O=C(C(F)(F)F)CCCC=Cc1ccccc1 gave empty result. Maybe need to include "C-C double bonds" broken and "five-membered rings" formed. Let's try again with correct SMILES for precursor: O=C(C(F)(F)F)C1CC(C=Cc2ccccc2)CC1.
